Created by `CreateDocumentTypeFolders`. Sort every new document type into one of them: - **Page** — a document that renders. May use compositions. - **Block** — element for block list/grid. Renders. Never used as a composition. - **Composition** — element only composed onto others. Never rendered, never pickable. Never put real content behind a composition (removing a composition permanently deletes its content). - **Data** — element that never renders (settings, events, people). - **Repository** — document that never renders; a container/root node. The content root is always a Repository. - **Repository Item** — document that never renders; the pickable records inside a Repository. 2. **The content root is a Repository**: `siteRoot` (in the Repositories folder) is the only allowed root type; a published "WWW" node is created on first boot. Add sites as Pages beneath it — you are multi-site ready by default. - **Give the site Page a domain, or nothing answers on `/`.** WWW never renders, so the first real page is a child and Umbraco routes it under its node name (`/blog/`) until a domain says otherwise. For a single site, assign it the domain `/`; for several, give each its own hostname. Over MCP that is one call: `put-document-domains` with `{ "defaultIsoCode": "en-US", "domains": [{ "domainName": "/", "isoCode": "en-US" }] }`. 3. **Data types are never at the folder root**: `DataTypeSavedHandler` (in `Notifications/`) moves every data type saved at root into `/Umbraco/` (built-in) or `/Custom/` (yours). The migration organizes the shipped ones on first boot. 4. **Compose in `Composers/`, not Program.cs.** Program.cs stays as scaffolded; non-Umbraco concerns go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods. 5. **Production runs in production mode**: `appsettings.json` is Production (models Nothing, UseHttps, no template editing); `appsettings.Development.json` is where development conveniences live. 6. **Aliases are English camelCase.** Translation keys are PascalCase dot-separated (`My.Dictionary.Item`); folders have no values themselves. Media lives in folders. 7. **uSync everything** (installed, version matched to the Umbraco major). On Umbraco Cloud use Umbraco Deploy instead. ## ModelsBuilder SourceCodeAuto in development. Generated models land in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/Models/ModelsBuilder/` with namespace `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco.Models`. Never edit generated files; extend via partials next to them. **When you change schema over MCP, generated models hit the disk immediately but the running site is still on the old assembly.** So work in this order: 1. **Model** — document types, element types, data types, templates, allowed children. 2. **Content** — create and publish. Still the old assembly; MCP doesn't care. 3. **Stop the site, `dotnet build`, restart.** The running site holds a lock on `bin/…/*.exe`, so a build while it runs fails with MSB3027. 4. **Razor** — only now do the models exist to compile against. # Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

Photo by Christopher Gower on Unsplash." - richText contentKey: 69c4b315-0248-427e-a7cd-c9d24e052e6c - body markup: more paragraphs Post 1 richtext 1 markup: ```html

MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is the thing that lets an AI agent actually do stuff in the real world: read your files, query your database, drive your CMS, post to your chat. Before MCP, every integration was a bespoke adapter written twice — once for the tool, once for the model. MCP replaces all of that with one open standard.

One protocol, every tool

A tool server speaks MCP once, and every MCP-capable client — Claude, Cursor, your own scripts — can use it. Write the server, get the whole ecosystem. That is the same network effect that made HTTP and USB win, applied to agent tooling.

  • Tools — functions the agent can call, with typed schemas.
  • Resources — read-only data the agent can browse, like files or records.
  • Prompts — reusable prompt templates the server shares with clients.
``` Post 1 richtext 2 markup: ```html

Your agent, your rules

Because the client is the one calling the tools, you stay in control: every call is visible, every permission can be scoped, and nothing happens without the agent asking. MCP turns "the AI did something" into "the AI asked, and I said yes".

And because the protocol is transport-agnostic and JSON-based, it works the same whether the server runs on your laptop over stdio or in the cloud over HTTP. Local dev and production are the same code.

``` **Post 2** — "MCP Made This Blog Possible" (blogPost, parent Home): - summary: "This entire site — schema, blocks, posts, images — was built by an agent talking to Umbraco over MCP. No backoffice clicks required." - publishDate: "2026-10-09" - blocks: hero + richText + image + richText - hero contentKey: c5e2e484-890e-4311-865c-f295c9bdc028 - heading: "MCP Made This Blog Possible" - subheading: "Schema, content, media — an agent built this whole site by talking to Umbraco over MCP." - backgroundImage: mediaKey 51290c54-01d9-4578-b2b3-66e5823700e1, key 19542dc7-22e5-4f88-97bb-5f70eeb36229 - richText contentKey: 3238ecdb-1259-436b-84b9-6fbd335ab494 - image contentKey: 44594bb2-dcae-4adb-aba0-cacebbf8f5cd - image: mediaKey 815039bc-31ff-452d-ac5b-8c81dedc83a6, key 7ec1b89f-a263-41c7-9d6d-6cfb8fc0604a - caption: "Under the hood of every good integration. Photo by Alexandre Debiève on Unsplash." - richText contentKey: a493df0a-aaa9-4f86-b1ef-c5346d2ac4f9 Post 2 richtext 1: ```html

This blog — the document types, the block element types, the templates, these very words, the photos — was created end to end by an agent talking to Umbraco's management API over MCP. Not one click in the backoffice.

Schema first, content second

The agent modeled the schema first: a Blog Front Page and a Blog Post document type, plus three block element types — hero, rich text, image — all filed into the right folders by the project's own rules. Only then did it create content, because content needs a schema to land in.

``` Post 2 richtext 2: ```html

Blocks all the way down

Every page body is a block grid. The hero, the paragraphs, the photos — all blocks, rendered by Umbraco's own pipeline, each block a small view component behind a thin adapter partial. No custom renderers, no wrapper models — just Umbraco's conventions.

Then: stop the site, rebuild so the generated models exist, write the Razor, restart. Three steps, one pipeline, and a blog that renders. That is MCP being awesome — the agent did the plumbing so the site could just exist.

``` Home summary... blogFrontPage has no summary property — only blocks. Good. Now create documents. create-document params: documentTypeId, parentId, name, templateId (optional — default template applied automatically; I'll omit and let default apply... actually safer to pass templateId explicitly? "If omitted, the document type's default template is applied automatically." Omit — default is set.), values: [{ editorAlias?, culture, segment, alias, value }]. The values schema in create-document: { editorAlias, culture, segment, alias, value } — all required per schema but editorAlias maybe optional in practice. I'll include alias, culture: null, segment: null, value. Include editorAlias too? The schema lists editorAlias as a property (string). For create-document the value items require editorAlias, culture, segment, alias, value per the JSON schema "required". Hmm, the tool schema says required: ["editorAlias", "culture", "segment", "alias", "value"]. I'll include editorAlias with the property editor alias: for blocks → "Umbraco.BlockGrid", summary → "Umbraco.TextBox", publishDate → "Umbraco.DateTime". Hmm — is editorAlias needed? The update-document-properties tool only needs alias. For create-document, schema requires it. I'll provide them. Wait, actually — does editorAlias matter for value parsing? Umbraco's create content model: values have alias + value; editorAlias isn't part of Umbraco's API (it's the MCP wrapper's addition, maybe used to shape the value). I'll include it; harmless. <Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <CompressionEnabled>false</CompressionEnabled> <!-- Disable compression. E.g. for umbraco backoffice files. These files should be precompressed by node and not let dotnet handle it -->
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Umbraco.Cms" />
    <PackageReference Include="uSync" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <!--
      Opt-in to app-local ICU to ensure consistent globalization APIs across different platforms.
      Default mirrors prior behaviour introduced in https://github.com/umbraco/Umbraco-CMS/pull/11276: enabled unless building on macOS without an explicit RuntimeIdentifier.
      To override:
        * Build/publish:  dotnet publish -p:UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu=false
        * Post-publish:   edit System.Globalization.AppLocalIcu in the published *.runtimeconfig.json
      Note: DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_APPLOCALICU is only honored when AppLocalIcu is absent from runtimeconfig.json
      (verified on .NET 10) — the general .NET 9 env-var-precedence rule does not apply to this knob, since it is
      resolved by the native host before the CLR boots. Use one of the two override paths above instead.
      Keep UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion in sync with the referenced Microsoft.ICU.ICU4C.Runtime package version.
    -->
    <UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == '' and ($(RuntimeIdentifier.StartsWith('linux')) or $(RuntimeIdentifier.StartsWith('win')) or ('$(RuntimeIdentifier)' == '' and !$([MSBuild]::IsOSPlatform('osx'))))">true</UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu>
    <UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == ''">false</UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu>
    <UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion Condition="'$(UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion)' == ''">72.1.0.3</UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == 'true'">
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.ICU.ICU4C.Runtime" />
    <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="System.Globalization.AppLocalIcu" Value="$(UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion)" />
  </ItemGroup>


  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- Razor files are needed for the backoffice to work correctly -->
    <CopyRazorGenerateFilesToPublishDirectory>true</CopyRazorGenerateFilesToPublishDirectory>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- Keep the local appsettings.json override out of publish output -->
    <Content Update="appsettings.Local.json" CopyToPublishDirectory="Never" />
  </ItemGroup>


</Project>

MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is what lets an AI agent actually do things in the real world: read your files, query your database, drive your CMS, post to your chat. Before MCP, every one of those integrations was a bespoke adapter, written twice — once for the tool, once for the model. MCP replaces all of that with a single open standard.

One protocol, every tool

A tool server speaks MCP once, and every MCP-capable client — Claude, Cursor, your own scripts — can use it. Write the server, get the whole ecosystem. It is the same network effect that made HTTP and USB win, applied to agent tooling.

  • Tools — functions the agent can call, with typed schemas.
  • Resources — read-only data the agent can browse, like files or records.
  • Prompts — reusable prompt templates a server shares with its clients.
``` Post 1 richtext 2 markup: ```html

Your agent, your rules

Because the client is the one calling the tools, you stay in control: every call is visible, every permission can be scoped, and nothing happens unless the agent asks. MCP turns "the AI did something" into "the AI asked, and I said yes".

And because the protocol is JSON-based and transport-agnostic, it works the same whether the server runs on your laptop over stdio or in the cloud over HTTP. Local dev and production are the same code.

This blog — the document types, the block element types, the templates, these very words, the photos — was created end to end by an agent talking to Umbraco's management API over MCP. Not one click in the backoffice.

Schema first, content second

The agent modeled the schema before writing a word: a Blog Front Page and a Blog Post document type, plus three block element types — hero, rich text, image — each filed into the right folder by the project's own rules. Only then did it create content, because content needs a schema to land in.

``` Post 2 richtext 2: ```html

Blocks all the way down

Every page body is a block grid. The hero, the paragraphs, the photos — all blocks, rendered by Umbraco's own pipeline, each block a small view component behind a thin adapter partial. No custom renderers, no wrapper models — just Umbraco's conventions.

Then the pipeline: stop the site, rebuild so the generated models exist, write the Razor, restart. Three steps, one flow, and a blog that renders. That is MCP being awesome — the agent did the plumbing so the site could simply exist.

value.markup:
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is what lets an AI agent actually do things in the real world: read your files, query your database, drive your CMS, post to your chat. Before MCP, every one of those integrations was a bespoke adapter, written twice — once for the tool, once for the model. MCP replaces all of that with a single open standard.

One protocol, every tool

A tool server speaks MCP once, and every MCP-capable client — Claude, Cursor, your own scripts — can use it. Write the server, get the whole ecosystem. It is the same network effect that made HTTP and USB win, applied to agent tooling.

  • Tools — functions the agent can call, with typed schemas.
  • Resources — read-only data the agent can browse, like files or records.
  • Prompts — reusable prompt templates a server shares with its clients.

value.markup:
Your agent, your rules

Because the client is the one calling the tools, you stay in control: every call is visible, every permission can be scoped, and nothing happens unless the agent asks. MCP turns "the AI did something" into "the AI asked, and I said yes".

And because the protocol is JSON-based and transport-agnostic, it works the same whether the server runs on your laptop over stdio or in the cloud over HTTP. Local dev and production are the same code.

values.value: One open standard between AI agents and the tools they use — and why it changes how software gets built.
Why the Model Context Protocol Is Awesome
One standard between agents and tools — and it changes how software gets built.

value.markup:
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is what lets an AI agent actually do things in the real world: read your files, query your database, drive your CMS, post to your chat. Before MCP, every one of those integrations was a bespoke adapter, written twice — once for the tool, once for the model. MCP replaces all of that with a single open standard.

One protocol, every tool

A tool server speaks MCP once, and every MCP-capable client — Claude, Cursor, your own scripts — can use it. Write the server, get the whole ecosystem. It is the same network effect that made HTTP and USB win, applied to agent tooling.

  • Tools — functions the agent can call, with typed schemas.
  • Resources — read-only data the agent can browse, like files or records.
  • Prompts — reusable prompt templates a server shares with its clients.

values.value: Where the agent does the typing. Photo by Christopher Gower on Unsplash.

value.markup:
Your agent, your rules

Because the client is the one calling the tools, you stay in control: every call is visible, every permission can be scoped, and nothing happens unless the agent asks. MCP turns "the AI did something" into "the AI asked, and I said yes".

And because the protocol is JSON-based and transport-agnostic, it works the same whether the server runs on your laptop over stdio or in the cloud over HTTP. Local dev and production are the same code.

Done. The blog is built, published, and verified over HTTP. The site is left running.

## Report

**What was built** — a two-post blog on the Umbraco.Bench scaffold, modeled, created, and rendered entirely through the MCP server (no backoffice clicks, no migration plans):

- **Schema** (all via MCP, filed per the UmbraCommandments):
  - Element types in `Blocks/`: `heroBlock` (heading, subheading, background image), `richTextBlock` (Tiptap body), `imageBlock` (image + caption) — created at root, moved into `Blocks` (`create-element-type` takes no `parentId`).
  - Data type `Blog Blocks` (`Umbraco.BlockGrid`) referencing the three blocks; reused shipped data types (Textstring, Richtext, Image Media Picker, Date Picker) — no new ones needed.
  - Pages in `Pages/`: `blogFrontPage` (block grid; allows `blogPost` children) and `blogPost` (summary, publishDate, block grid). Templates `BlogFrontPage`/`BlogPost` created first, then attached via whole-object `update-document-type` merges; `siteRoot` updated to allow `blogFrontPage`.
- **Content**: media folder `Blog` with 5 Unsplash photos imported from `unsplash/` (credits in captions); `The MCP Blog` front page under `WWW` with domain `/`; two published posts — *"Why the Model Context Protocol Is Awesome"* and *"MCP Made This Blog Possible"* — each a block grid of hero → rich text → image → rich text. Every document read back over MCP to confirm values landed.
- **Rendering** (after stop → `dotnet build` → restart, per the required order): page views `Views/BlogFrontPage.cshtml` / `Views/BlogPost.cshtml`; adapter-only partials `Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components/{heroBlock,richTextBlock,imageBlock}.cshtml` mapping `BlockGridItem<T>` to plain models in `Models/Blocks/`; ViewComponents (`Hero`, `RichText`, `Image`) with views in `Views/Shared/Components/`; friendly extensions only (`Children<BlogPost>()`, `GetCropUrl`, `GetBlockGridHtmlAsync`); `.richtext` typography added to `site.css`; frontend rebuilt so Tailwind picked up the new classes.

**How to view it**: https://localhost:44317/ (front page + post listing) — posts at `/why-the-model-context-protocol-is-awesome/` and `/mcp-made-this-blog-possible/`. Backoffice at `/umbraco` (admin@example.com / 1234567890).

**Verified working**: all three pages HTTP 200; hero, both rich-text sections, captioned images with signed crop URLs, dates, and post links all present; zero "Could not render component" fallbacks; media and `dist/site.css` serve 200; content tree and publish state confirmed over MCP after restart.

**Not working / quirks worth knowing** (nothing broken, but three MCP-server behaviors cost a retry each):
1. On Umbraco 18 the block-grid `layout` is `"Umbraco.BlockGrid": [ …items… ]` (array directly) — the older `{"items":[…]}` wrapper is rejected with a 500; `validate-document` confirmed the fix before creating content.
2. `create-document` silently drops block-item `properties` (they read back empty) — block properties must be set with `update-block-property`, which works reliably.
3. `create-template` rejects `content` containing `?` or `&` (so no `?.` or HTML entities in DB template content); the Razor files in `Views/` are the render source of truth and take precedence anyway.
